reasons: Lake identity is verified for Mancusi v. DeForte, U.S. Supreme Court, decided 1968-06-17, year 1968.

defect.evidence_quote: We hold that in these circumstances DeForte had Fourth Amendment standing to object to the admission of the papers at his trial.
defect.problem: The holding is supported, but as phrased it is slightly broader than the opinion's explicitly circumstance-bound holding because it omits that DeForte spent considerable time in the shared office and had custody of the seized records.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: In these circumstances, DeForte, a union official who spent considerable time in a shared office and had custody of the seized records, had Fourth Amendment standing to challenge the warrantless office search because the inquiry turned on reasonable expectation of freedom from governmental intrusion, not property title.

reasons: The opinion supports the core rule: capacity to claim Fourth Amendment protection depends on reasonable expectation of freedom from governmental intrusion, not property right.
The opinion supports the shared-office application: DeForte could reasonably expect only the officials and their guests would enter and records would not be touched without permission.
The phrase 'in these circumstances' limits the holding more than the current summary does.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add the circumstance limits: shared office, considerable time there, custody of seized records, and no consent.

reasons: The opinion expressly frames the issue as whether DeForte had Fourth Amendment standing to object to the seizure of records from his office.
The Court held DeForte had standing and reasoned from Jones and Katz, supporting a Standing to Challenge a Search home role as a key progeny case.
residual_risks: No separate home page file was disclosed to verify local ordering or taxonomy beyond the case text and built page.
